Multiplying matrices via polynomials:
exposition and barriers We give an exposition of OpenAI’s recent proof that the exponent \(\omega_\mathbb{C}\) of matrix multiplication over the complex numbers satisfies \(\omega_\mathbb{C}\le 9/4\). Our version of the proof gives \(\omega_\mathbb{F}\le 9/4\) over every field F. We also treat the rectangular matrix multiplication exponent \(\omega_\mathbb{F}(a,b,c)\). Here we have \(\omega_\mathbb{F}(1,k,1)=2\) for \(0\le k\le 1/2\) and \(\omega_\mathbb{F}(1,k,1)\le 1+k+1/(4k)\) for \(k\ge 1/2\), and, for real numbers \(a\ge b\ge c\ge 0\), \(\omega_\mathbb{F}(a,b,c)=a+b\) if \(c(a+b)\le ab\) and \(\omega_\mathbb{F}(a,b,c)\le(a+b+c)/2+(ab/c+ac/b+bc/a)/4\) otherwise. Our exposition is in the language of degeneration inequalities among polynomial multiplication tensors and Strassen’s asymptotic spectrum duality. We moreover prove an operational barrier (which can be thought of as coming from an operational asymptotic spectrum) showing that the current analysis of all these upper bounds on \(\omega_\mathbb{F}\) and \(\omega_\mathbb{F}(a,b,c)\) is optimal and that in fact the current degeneration ingredients cannot improve the bounds. ## Contents **1 Introduction 2**

## 1 Introduction

The exponent \(\omega_\mathbb{F}\) of matrix multiplication over a field F is the infimum of all real numbers \(\tau\) such that the tensor rank of the matrix multiplication tensor \(\langle n,n,n\rangle\) over F is \(\mathcal{O}(n^\tau)\). OpenAI recently released a proof that \(\omega_\mathbb{C}\le 9/4\) \[Ope26a, Theorem 1.1\], significantly improving over the previous upper bounds and using new ideas. We give an exposition of their proof in the language of degeneration inequalities and Strassen’s asymptotic spectrum of tensors \[Str88, Section 3\] (see also the survey of Wigderson and Zuiddam \[WZ26\]). Our version of the proof works over every field.

**Theorem 1.1.** _For every field_ F, \(\omega_\mathbb{F}\le 9/4\).

The previous upper bound was \(\omega_\mathbb{F}<2.371339\) \[ADW<sup>+</sup>25\], from the laser method.

We also discuss rectangular matrix multiplication exponents. For integers \(n_1,n_2,n_3\ge 1\), the matrix multiplication tensor \(\langle n_1,n_2,n_3\rangle\) describes the multiplication of an \(n_1\times n_2\) matrix by an \(n_2\times n_3\) matrix. For real numbers \(a,b,c\ge 0\), let \(\omega_\mathbb{F}(a,b,c)\) be the infimum of the real numbers \(\gamma\) such that the tensor rank of \(\langle\lceil n^a\rceil,\lceil n^b\rceil,\lceil n^c\rceil\rangle\) over F is \(\mathcal{O}(n^\gamma)\). In particular, \(\omega_\mathbb{F}=\omega_\mathbb{F}(1,1,1)\). Following Uzna ́nski \[Uzn26\], the same methods give the following bounds.

**Theorem 1.2.** _For every field_ F _and all real numbers_ \(a\ge b\ge c\ge 0\),

\(\omega_\mathbb{F}(a,b,c)\le\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
a+b & \text{\textit{if}}c(a+b)\le ab, \\
\frac{(ab+bc+ca)^2}{4abc} & \text{\textit{if}}c(a+b)>ab,
\end{array}\right.\)

_with equality if_ \(c(a+b)\le ab\).

In particular, \(\omega_\mathbb{F}(1,k,1)=2\) for \(0\le k\le 1/2\), so \(\alpha_\mathbb{F}:=sup\{k\ge 0:\omega_\mathbb{F}(1,k,1)=2\}\) is at least 1/2 (Corollary 4.17). This implies for instance that \(n^2\times n\) by \(n\times n^2\) matrices can be multiplied in \(\mathcal{O}(n^{4+\varepsilon})\) operations! This improves previous \(\alpha_\mathbb{C}>0.465\) \[Ope26b\] and \(\alpha_\mathbb{F}>0.321334\) from the laser method \[WXXZ24\]. Figure 1 shows Theorem 1.2.

We will prove that the bound of Theorem 1.2 is "the best that its proof can give": the ingredients that our proof use do not give a better upper bound on \(\omega_\mathbb{F}(a,b,c)\), and neither does any combination (in a precise way) of the ingredients (Theorem 5.4). To improve the bounds further requires going around this "operational barrier".

In this introduction we will give a brief overview of the proof ideas and results, focussing on \(\omega_\mathbb{F}=\omega_\mathbb{F}(1,1,1)\), but the ideas work for the rectangular exponents \(\omega_\mathbb{F}(a,b,c)\) as well. Formal definitions and statements are from Section 2 onwards. Standard references for background are the survey of Bläser \[Blä13\] and the book of Bürgisser, Clausen and Shokrollahi \[BCS97\].

## 1.1 Degeneration ingredients and combination rules

The matrix multiplication tensor is \(\langle n_1,n_2,n_3\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_2}\sum_{k=1}^{n_3}E_{ij}\otimes E_{jk}\otimes E_{ki}\), where _E<sub>ij</sub>_ is the matrix with entry 1 at (_i,j_) and 0 elsewhere. The matrix multiplication exponent \(\omega_\mathbb{F}\) is defined in terms of tensor rank (or equivalently in terms of arithmetic circuit complexity). For a tensor _T_ the tensor rank R(_T_) is the smallest number _r_ such that \(T\le\langle r\rangle\) where \(\langle r\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^re_i\otimes e_i\otimes e_i\) is the unit tensor and where \(\le\) denotes restriction: the left hand side is obtained from the right hand side by applying linear maps to the three legs. It goes back to Strassen \[Str69\] that if \(\langle n,n,n\rangle\le\langle r\rangle\) for integers \(n\ge 2\) and \(r\ge 1\), then \(\omega_\mathbb{F}\le\mathrm{log}r/\mathrm{log}n\). Throughout, log denotes the logarithm to base 2.

It is known that \(\omega_\mathbb{F}\) does not change if we replace restriction by its approximative version, degeneration (i.e., we replace tensor rank by border rank): if \(\langle n,n,n\rangle\unknown\langle r\rangle\) for integers \(n\ge 2\) and \(r\ge 1\), then still \(\omega_\mathbb{F}\le\mathrm{log}r/\mathrm{log}n\). Degeneration \(\unknown\) is a restriction in which we allow to use matrices whose entries are polynomials in a formal variable \(\varepsilon\), which we think of as going to zero (also in positive characteristic one can define this correctly, symbolically). So to prove upper bounds on \(\omega_\mathbb{F}\) it suffices to prove degenerations of the form<tbc>

We may think of \(\le\) and \(\triangleleft\) as notions of reduction between computational problems, in this case using _r_ pairwise scalar multiplications to compute \(n\times n\) matrix multiplication, and we will see many more. Restriction \(S\le T\) implies degeneration \(S\triangleleft T\), but in our analysis (following Strassen’s way of working) we will go even further and use the asymptotic restriction \(S\lesssim T\) defined by \(S^{\otimes n}\le T^{\otimes n}\otimes\langle 2^{o(n)}\rangle\), for which \(S\triangleleft T\) implies \(S\lesssim T\). (Indeed, also \(\langle n,n,n\rangle\lesssim\langle r\rangle\) implies \(\omega_\mathbb{F}\le\mathrm{log}r/\mathrm{log}n\).)

We explain the proof at a high level in terms of degenerations. We first discuss the ingredients. The main objects, besides the matrix multiplication tensors, are the polynomial multiplication tensors P_<sub>a,b</sub>_, which describe the multiplication of a polynomial of degree at most _a_-1 by a polynomial of degree at most _b_-1. In other words, with _e<sub>i</sub>_ standing for the monomial _t_<sup>_i_-1</sup>,

\(\mathsf{P}_{a,b}=\sum_{i=1}^a\sum_{j=1}^be_i\otimes e_j\otimes e_{i+j-1}\in\mathbb{F}^a\otimes\mathbb{F}^b\otimes\mathbb{F}^{a+b-1}.\)

## 1.1.1 Degeneration ingredients

The starting point is that the simplest kind of polynomial multiplication (multiplying a degree 0 polynomial with a degree _b_-1 polynomial, i.e. P<sub>1_,b_</sub>) is the same thing as the simplest kind of rectangular matrix multiplication (multiplying a constant with a length _b_ vector, i.e. \(\langle 1,1,b\rangle\)):

(D0) **Matrix multiplication.** \(\mathsf{P}_{1,b}\cong\langle 1,1,b\rangle\) (Definition 3.1).

By ingredient (D0), and since \(\langle k,\ell,m\rangle\cong\langle k,1,1\rangle\otimes\langle 1,\ell,1\rangle\otimes\langle 1,1,m\rangle\), we see that the semiring, with direct sum \(\oplus\) as addition and tensor product \(\otimes\) as multiplication, generated by the polynomial multiplication tensors P_<sub>a,b</sub>_ and their permutations (where we mean permuting the three tensor legs), contains all matrix multiplication tensors \(\langle n_1,n_2,n_3\rangle\), and their direct sums. It will thus be natural to study the matrix multiplication tensors through (permuted) polynomial multiplication tensors.

Next, what makes polynomial multiplication appealing, is the fundamental fact that polynomial multiplication is computationally very cheap (by interpolation!), which in our language corresponds to a border rank upper bound:

(D1) **Border rank.** \(\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\triangleleft\langle a+b-1\rangle\) (Proposition 3.2).

In the study of matrix multiplication, as we already hinted at above, tensors are commonly combined by the direct sum \(\oplus\) and the tensor product \(\otimes\). Tensor products are natural because \(\langle n_1,n_2,n_3\rangle\otimes\langle m_1,m_2,m_3\rangle\cong\langle n_1m_1,n_2m_2,n_3m_3\rangle\) ( "block matrices are multiplied blockwise"). Direct sums are natural because of Schönhage’s asymptotic sum inequality: if \(\langle n_1,n_1,n_1\rangle\oplus\cdots\oplus\langle n_p,n_p,n_p\rangle\triangleleft\langle r\rangle\) for integers \(p,n_1,\dots,n_p,r\ge 1\), then we can obtain from this degenerations of the form \(\langle m,m,m\rangle\triangleleft\langle s\rangle\) that imply \(n_1^{\omega_\mathbb{F}}+\cdots+n_p^{\omega_\mathbb{F}}\le r\) \[Sch81, Theorem 7.1\]. So a direct sum of matrix multiplication tensors that is a degeneration of a unit tensor also bounds \(\omega_\mathbb{F}\), like the degenerations \(\langle n,n,n\rangle\triangleleft\langle r\rangle\) above.

Now if we look at \(T\otimes\langle 1,1,2\rangle\) we see that this gives a notion of partial direct sum of _T_ with itself, which we denote by \(T\oplus_1T\): two copies of _T_ are placed next to each other with one shared leg and two disjoint legs. More generally \(\oplus_1\) denotes a partial direct sum, whose summands share their first leg (Section 2.1).

We will be working a lot with these partial direct sums \(\oplus_1\), but in the end we will need a way to transform these back into the usual world of direct sums \(\oplus\):

(D2) **Separating partial direct sums into direct sums.** For a partial direct sum \(T_1\oplus_1\cdots\oplus_1T_m\) and every integer \(t\ge 1\),<tbc>

<tbc>\((T_1\oplus\cdots\oplus T_m)\otimes\mathsf{P}_{1,t}\unknown(T_1\oplus_1\cdots\oplus_1T_m)\otimes\mathsf{P}_{m,t}\)<tbc>

<tbc>(Proposition 3.5).

Note how ingredient (D2) turns a partial direct sum into a direct sum, at the cost of turning a factor P_<sub>m,t</sub>_ into P<sub>1_,t_</sub>, thus using P_<sub>m,t</sub>_ as a "partially consumed catalyst" for this degeneration.

Finally, we need two families of degenerations that relate partial direct sums of polynomial multiplication tensors. The first family is:

(D3) **Concavity degeneration.** For \(b\ge 2\), \(\mathsf{P}_{a,b+1}\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{a,b-1}\triangleup_1\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\), and the same with arbitrary \(\oplus_1C\) added on both sides (Lemma 3.6).<tbc>

<tbc>(Here the subscript in \(\triangleup_1\) indicates that these degenerations do not act on the first leg, which indeed allows adding arbitrary \(\oplus_1C\) on both sides.) In terms of polynomials, ingredient (D3) is using two multiplications of the same polynomial _f_ by polynomials of degree at most _b_-1 to compute multiplications of _f_ by polynomials of degree at most _b_ and _b_-2. The construction of (D3) is related to the representation theory of SL<sub>2</sub>.

The second family is:

(D4) **Tripling degeneration.** \(\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\oplus_1((23)\cdot\mathsf{P}_{a,b})\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\triangleup_1\mathsf{P}_{a,3b+a-1}\), where \((23)\cdot\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\) is P_<sub>a,b</sub>_ with its second and third legs exchanged; and again the same with arbitrary \(\oplus_1C\) added on both sides (Lemma 3.11).

In terms of polynomials, ingredient (D4) is using one multiplication of _f_ by a polynomial _g_ of degree at most 3_b+a_-2 to compute three smaller ones. We can use the lowest _b_ and the highest _b_ coefficients of _g_ to do two multiplications of _f_ by polynomials of degree at most _b_-1, the two copies of P_<sub>a,b</sub>_. Using degeneration we are able to squeeze in an extra, permuted polynomial multiplication, \((23)\cdot\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\).

## 1.1.2 Combination rules

The proof will combine the above degeneration ingredients (D0)-(D4) by basic combination rules to obtain more degenerations, as to eventually obtain degenerations of the form \(\langle n,n,n\rangle\unknown\langle r\rangle\), hopefully such that log_r/_log_n_ is small. These rules are:

(C1) reflexivity: \(T\triangleup T\);<tbc>

(C2) transitivity: if \(T_1\triangleup T_2\) and \(T_2\triangleup T_3\), then \(T_1\triangleup T_3\);<tbc>

(C3) direct sums and tensor products: if \(T_1\triangleup S_1\) and \(T_2\triangleup S_2\), then \(T_1\oplus T_2\triangleup S_1\oplus S_2\) and \(T_1\otimes T_2\triangleup S_1\otimes S_2\);<tbc>

(C4) permutations of the legs: if \(T\triangleleft S\), then \(\pi\cdot T\triangleleft\pi\cdot S\) for every permutation \(\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3\) of the three legs.

Finding the optimal combination of the degeneration ingredients given these combination rules seems a daunting task! Not only do we have an infinite family of degeneration ingredients (parametrised by the several parameters _a,b,t,m_), we may also need to use large _n_ to obtain our target degenerations \(\langle n,n,n\rangle\triangleleft\langle r\rangle\) for which log_r/_log_n_ is small.

Let us first illustrate what sort of combination strategies we may want to do, and then let Strassen’s asymptotic spectrum duality come to the rescue to turn this into a tractable optimisation problem (with a clean analysis, optimal objective value and "dual certificate").

## 1.2 Understanding how the ingredients can be combined

Let us try to combine the degeneration ingredients according to the combination rules to start understanding them, including the role of catalysts and asymptotics.

### 1.2.1 From P_<sub>a,b</sub>_ to partial direct sum of \(\langle 1,1,n\rangle\) and permutations

Fix an integer \(a\ge 2\). By ingredient (D1), we have \(\langle 2a-1\rangle\triangleleft\mathsf{P}_{a,a}\). Tensoring both sides with \(\langle 1,1,n\rangle\) gives

\(\langle 2a-1\rangle\otimes\langle 1,1,n\rangle\triangleleft\mathsf{P}_{a,a}\otimes\langle 1,1,n\rangle\cong\mathsf{P}_{a,a}\oplus_1\cdots\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{a,a},\) (1.1)

the partial direct sum of _n_ copies of P_<sub>a,a</sub>_.

Ingredients (D3) and (D4) are degenerations that act only on the second and third legs, so they can be applied to some of the summands of a partial direct sum while the other summands stay as they are. With ingredient (D3), the second parameter branches out: two summands P_<sub>a,b</sub>_ become P<sub>_a,b_+1</sub> and P<sub>_a,b_-1</sub>. For example, ingredient (D3) with _b=a_, applied to two of the summands, continues (1.1):<tbc>

\(\mathsf{P}_{a,a}\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{a,a}\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{a,a}\oplus_1\cdots\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{a,a}\triangleleft\mathsf{P}_{a,a+1}\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{a,a-1}\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{a,a}\oplus_1\cdots\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{a,a}.\)

<tbc>With ingredient (D4), a summand P<sub>_a,_3_b+a_-1</sub> with a large second parameter 3_b+a_-1 becomes three summands with second parameter _b_, one of them with its second and third legs exchanged. In this way one can reach summands with second parameter 1, which are matrix multiplication tensors, since \(\mathsf{P}_{a,1}\cong\langle a,1,1\rangle\) and \((23)\cdot\mathsf{P}_{a,1}\cong\langle 1,a,1\rangle\). For example, a summand P<sub>_a,a_+2</sub>, which three applications of ingredient (D3) produce from four copies of P_<sub>a,a</sub>_, becomes three matrix multiplication tensors by ingredient (D4) with _b_=1:

\(\mathsf{P}_{a,a+2}\triangleleft\mathsf{P}_{a,1}\oplus_1((23)\cdot\mathsf{P}_{a,1})\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{a,1}\cong\langle a,1,1\rangle\oplus_1\langle 1,a,1\rangle\oplus_1\langle a,1,1\rangle.\)

All in all, we see that after (1.1), applying (D3) and (D4) will let us produce certain partial direct sums of matrix multiplication tensors.

### 1.2.2 From partial direct sums to \(\langle n,n,n\rangle\) via symmetrisation and powering

Suppose that in the above manner the _n_ copies of P_<sub>a,a</sub>_ of (1.1) become a partial direct sum that contains _s_ copies of \(\langle a,1,1\rangle\) and _t_ copies of \(\langle 1,a,1\rangle\). (Note that here we have not yet specified explicitly what _s_ and _t_ can be; applying the above ideas cleverly will have to optimise this; We will discuss this via an example in a moment.) The partial direct sum of the _s_ copies of \(\langle a,1,1\rangle\) is \(\langle a,1,1\rangle\otimes\langle 1,1,s\rangle\cong\langle a,1,s\rangle\), and likewise the partial direct sum of the _t_ copies of \(\langle 1,a,1\rangle\) is \(\langle 1,a,t\rangle\). Together with (1.1), this gives<tbc>

\(\langle 2a-1\rangle\otimes\langle 1,1,n\rangle\triangleleft\langle a,1,s\rangle\oplus_1\langle 1,a,t\rangle.\) (1.2)

To make the matrix multiplication tensors appearing in (1.2) "square" (i.e., of the form \(\langle p,p,p\rangle\)), we use the symmetrisation operation \(\otimes_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3}\pi\cdot T\) for any tensor _T_, the tensor product of the six tensors obtained from _T_ by permuting its legs. For all integers \(k,\ell,m\ge 1\),<tbc>

\(\otimes_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3}\pi\cdot\langle k,\ell,m\rangle\cong\langle k\ell m,k\ell m,k\ell m\rangle^{\otimes 2},\)

<tbc>which depends only on the product \(k\ell m\). In particular, the symmetrisation of \(\langle 1,1,n\rangle\) is \(\langle n,n,n\rangle^{\otimes 2}\), and that of \(\langle 2a-1\rangle\) is \(\langle 2a-1\rangle^{\otimes 6}\). So symmetrising both sides of (1.2) gives

\(\langle 2a-1\rangle^{\otimes 6}\otimes\langle n,n,n\rangle^{\otimes 2}\supseteq\otimes_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3}\pi\cdot\big(\langle a,1,s\rangle\oplus_1\langle 1,a,t\rangle\big).\) (1.3)

From the right-hand side of (1.3) we will construct an asymptotic restriction to one square matrix multiplication tensor (in a manner reminiscent of the laser method, but simpler):

\(\otimes_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3}\pi\cdot\big(\langle a,1,s\rangle\oplus_1\langle 1,a,t\rangle\big)\unknown\langle a(s+t),a(s+t),a(s+t)\rangle^{\otimes 2}.\) (1.4)

The idea of the proof of (1.4) is to take the _N_th tensor power of \(\langle a,1,s\rangle\oplus_1\langle 1,a,t\rangle\), for large _N_, and to keep only its summands with a fixed number _k_ of factors \(\langle a,1,s\rangle\). These are \(h:=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{N}{k}\) tensors that share the first leg, each isomorphic to \(M:=\langle a^k,a^{N-k},s^kt^{N-k}\rangle\). By ingredients (D2) and (D1), with \(\mathsf{P}_{1,h}\cong\langle 1,1,h\rangle\) and \(\mathsf{P}_{h,h}\triangleleft\langle 2h-1\rangle\), their partial direct sum _Y_ satisfies

\(\langle h\rangle\otimes\big(M\otimes\langle 1,1,h\rangle\big)\triangleleft\langle 2h-1\rangle\otimes Y.\)

The left-hand side consists of _h_ copies of \(M\otimes\langle 1,1,h\rangle\), and the right-hand side of fewer than 2_h_ copies of _Y_ . The product of the three parameters of \(M\otimes\langle 1,1,h\rangle\) is \(a^N\genfrac(){pt}{2}{N}{k}s^kt^{N-k}\). For the _k_ at which \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{N}{k}s^kt^{N-k}\) is largest, this product is at least (_a(s+t_))_<sup>N</sup>/(N_+1), since the _N_+1 numbers \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{N}{k}s^kt^{N-k}\) add up to (_s+t)<sup>N</sup>_. The factors 2 and _N_+1 do not matter as \(N\rightarrow\infty\), and the symmetrisation makes the result square.

Composing the degeneration (1.3) and the asymptotic restriction (1.4) gives<tbc>

\(\langle 2a-1\rangle^{\otimes 6}\otimes\langle n,n,n\rangle^{\otimes 2}\unknown\langle a(s+t),a(s+t),a(s+t)\rangle^{\otimes 2}.\) (1.5)

<tbc>Suppose (essentially without loss of generality, after taking tensor powers and rounding down) that _a(s+t_)=_cn_ for an integer \(c\ge 2\). Then \(\langle cn,cn,cn\rangle\cong\langle c,c,c\rangle\otimes\langle n,n,n\rangle\), and (1.5) reads<tbc>

\(\langle 2a-1\rangle^{\otimes 6}\otimes\langle n,n,n\rangle^{\otimes 2}\unknown\langle c,c,c\rangle^{\otimes 2}\otimes\langle n,n,n\rangle^{\otimes 2}.\)

<tbc>Then \(\langle n,n,n\rangle^{\otimes 2}\) acts as a catalyst: it is needed as input, but also returned as an output. A common nonzero tensor factor can be cancelled in an asymptotic restriction \[WZ26, Lemmas 3.5 and 3.7\], which for us gives

\(\langle 2a-1\rangle^{\otimes 6}\unknown\langle c,c,c\rangle^{\otimes 2},\)

so \(\omega_\mathbb{F}\le 3log(2a-1)/logc\).

## 1.2.3 Concrete example of applying ingredients (D3) and (D4)

As a concrete example (already leading to a non-trivial upper bound on \(\omega_\mathbb{F}\)), we now carry out the above steps for _a_=2. Ingredients (D3) and (D4) turn four copies of P<sub>2,2</sub> into matrix<tbc>

multiplication tensors and one copy of P2,2: \(\mathsf{P}_{2,2}\otimes\langle 1,1,4\rangle\cong\mathsf{P}_{2,2}\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{2,2}\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{2,2}\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{2,2}\)
\(\supseteq\mathsf{P}_{2,1}\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{2,3}\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{2,3}\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{2,1}\) (D3), _b_=2, twice

## 1.4 Barriers for obtaining better bounds

We have seen how some combination of the degeneration ingredients gives \(\omega_\mathbb{F}\le 9/4\) (and in a similar way bounds on the rectangular matrix multiplication exponents). Can we do better? Not with current ingredients.

### 1.4.1 No barrier from irreversibility

First of all, standard barriers are not effective here. Christandl, Vrana and Zuiddam \[CVZ21, Theorem 3.1\] (see also Alman \[Alm19\] and Christandl, Le Gall, Lysikov and Zuiddam \[CLGLZ25\]) proved a barrier for upper bounds on \(\omega_\mathbb{F}\) from a fixed tensor _S_ (generalising previous barriers of Ambainis, Filmus and Le Gall \[AFLG15\]): every upper bound obtained from asymptotic restrictions \(\langle 2^n,2^n,2^n\rangle\lesssim S^{\otimes m}\) is at least 2irr(_S_), where the irreversibility irr(_S_) is the ratio of the logarithms of the asymptotic rank and the asymptotic subrank of _S_.

This irreversibility barrier does not explain why the proof of Theorem 1.1 gives no bound below 9/4: for the tensors \(S_a=\otimes_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3}\pi\cdot\mathsf{P}_{a,a}\) of (1.6), with \(a\ge 2\), the degenerations \(\langle a\rangle\unknown\mathsf{P}_{a,a}\unknown\langle 2a-1\rangle\) give \(\mathrm{irr}(S_a)\le\mathrm{log}(2a-1)/\mathrm{log}a\), so the barrier tends to the trivial value 2 as \(a\rightarrow\infty\). A similar analysis for rectangular matrix multiplication gives no irreversibility barrier there.

### 1.4.2 Tight barrier for (D0)-(D4)+(C1)-(C4)

No derivation from the ingredients (D0)-(D4) by the rules (C1)-(C4), with (D3) and (D4) also inside partial direct sums, gives an upper bound on \(\omega_\mathbb{F}\) below 9/4, and neither does a limit of such bounds (Theorem 5.4). This remains true for the asymptotic consequences of the rules, among them the asymptotic restriction (1.6). Likewise, for all real numbers \(a\ge b\ge c\ge 0\), no such derivation gives a better upper bound on \(\omega_\mathbb{F}(a,b,c)\) than Theorem 1.2.

## 2 Restriction and degeneration

In this section we define tensors, restrictions and degenerations, and state the facts about them that we will use. From now on, F is a field, and all vector spaces are finite-dimensional over F. We use the convention 0<sup>0</sup>=1, and for an integer \(n\ge 0\) we write \[_n_\]={1_,...,n_}.

### 2.1 Tensors

A _tensor_ over F is an element _T_ of a tensor product \(U\otimes V\otimes W\) of three vector spaces _U,V_ and _W_, which we call the first, second and third _leg_ of _T_. For tensors \(S\in U_1\otimes V_1\otimes W_1\) and \(T\in U_2\otimes V_2\otimes W_2\), the _direct sum_ \(S\oplus T\) lies in \((U_1\oplus U_2)\otimes(V_1\oplus V_2)\otimes(W_1\oplus W_2)\), and the _tensor product_ \(S\otimes T\) lies in \((U_1\otimes U_2)\otimes(V_1\otimes V_2)\otimes(W_1\otimes W_2)\), after regrouping the factors.

We define a version of the direct sum in which the first leg is shared. For an integer \(m\ge 1\), vector spaces _U_, _V_<sub>1</sub>_,...,V<sub>m</sub>_ and _W_<sub>1</sub>_,...,W<sub>m</sub>_, and tensors \(T_i\in U\otimes V_i\otimes W_i\) for \(i\in[m]\), their _partial direct sum_ is

\(T_1\oplus_1\cdots\oplus_1T_m:=T_1+\cdots+T_m\in U\otimes(V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_m)\otimes(W_1\oplus\cdots\oplus W_m).\)

Figure 2 compares the partial direct sum with the direct sum.

Let S<sub>3</sub> be the group of permutations of {1,2,3}. For a tensor \(T\in U\otimes V\otimes W\) and a permutation \(\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3\), let \(\pi\cdot T\) be the tensor obtained from _T_ by permuting the factors, so that, for every \(i\in\{1,2,3\}\), the _i_th leg of _T_ is the \(\pi(i)\)th leg of \(\pi\cdot T\), as in \[Str87, Section 2\].

For an integer \(n\ge 0\), let _e_<sub>1</sub>_,...,e<sub>n</sub>_ be the standard basis of F_<sup>n</sup>_. The _unit tensor_ is \(\langle n\rangle:=\sum_{i=1}^ne_i\otimes e_i\otimes e_i\). For integers \(n_1,n_2,n_3\ge 1\), the _matrix multiplication tensor_ is

\(\langle n_1,n_2,n_3\rangle:=\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_2}\sum_{k=1}^{n_3}E_{ij}\otimes E_{jk}\otimes E_{ki}\in\mathbb{F}^{n_1\times n_2}\otimes\mathbb{F}^{n_2\times n_3}\otimes\mathbb{F}^{n_3\times n_1},\)

where _E<sub>ij</sub>_ denotes the matrix with entry 1 at (_i,j_) and 0 elsewhere.

Generally, the tensor of a bilinear map \(\mu:U\times V\rightarrow W\) is \(T=\sum_{i,j}e_i^*\otimes e_j^*\otimes\mu(e_i,e_j)\) in \(U^*\otimes V^*\otimes W\), where the sums run over bases of _U_ and _V_ and \(e_i^*\) is the dual basis element of _e<sub>i</sub>_. We get \(\mu\) back from _T_ by evaluating the first two factors: \(\mu(u,v)=\sum_{i,j}e_i^*(u)e_j^*(v)\mu(e_i,e_j)\) for all \(u\in U\) and \(v\in V\) .

## 2.2 Restriction and tensor rank

Let \(S\in U_1\otimes V_1\otimes W_1\) and \(T\in U_2\otimes V_2\otimes W_2\) be tensors. Then _T_ is a _restriction_ of _S_, written \(T\le S\), if there are linear maps \(A_1:U_1\rightarrow U_2\), \(A_2:V_1\rightarrow V_2\) and \(A_3:W_1\rightarrow W_2\) such that \(T=(A_1\otimes A_2\otimes A_3)S\). If these maps can be chosen invertible, then _S_ and _T_ are _isomorphic_, written \(S\cong T\).

Two tensors are equivalent if each is a restriction of the other. Let S<sub>F</sub> be the set of equivalence classes. Strassen showed that direct sum and tensor product make S<sub>F</sub> a commutative semiring: both operations are associative and commutative and have identity elements, and the tensor product distributes over the direct sum \[Str87, Section 2\]. Restriction induces a partial order on S<sub>F</sub>, and it is compatible with both operations: if \(T_1\le S_1\) and \(T_2\le S_2\), then \(T_1\oplus T_2\le S_1\oplus S_2\) and \(T_1\otimes T_2\le S_1\otimes S_2\) \[Str87, Section 3\].

The _tensor rank_ R<sub>F</sub>(_T_) of a tensor \(T\in U\otimes V\otimes W\) is the least integer \(r\ge 0\) such that \(T=\sum_{i=1}^ru_i\otimes v_i\otimes w_i\) with \(u_i\in U\), \(v_i\in V\) and \(w_i\in W\) for \(i\in[r]\). The _exponent of matrix multiplication_ over F is

\(\omega_\mathbb{F}:=inf\{\tau\in\mathbb{R}:\mathrm{R}_\mathbb{F}(\langle n,n,n\rangle)=\mathcal{O}(n^\tau)\},\)

as in \[Str87, (1.3)\].

The _flattening ranks_ R<sub>(1)</sub>(_T_), R<sub>(2)</sub>(_T_) and R<sub>(3)</sub>(_T_) of a tensor \(T\in U\otimes V\otimes W\) are the matrix ranks of the images of _T_ in \(U\otimes(V\otimes W)\), \(V\otimes(U\otimes W)\) and \(W\otimes(U\otimes V)\).

\(T_{abc}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }

\end{array}\right.\)

Let _k_:=_k_<sub>1</sub>+_k_<sub>2</sub>+_k_<sub>3</sub>. Then \((A_1\otimes A_2\otimes A_3)S=\sum_{a,b,c}\varepsilon^{w_1(a)+w_2(b)+w_3(c)+k}S_{abc}e_a\otimes e_b\otimes e_c\). ## 3 Degenerations among polynomial multiplication tensors

In this section we will construct, over every field, the degenerations that the proofs of Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.2 use: degenerations between unit tensors and polynomial multiplication tensors (Section 3.1), the degeneration from a partial direct sum to a direct sum (Section 3.2), and two degenerations between polynomial multiplication tensors (Section 3.3 and Section 3.4).

## 3.1 Polynomial multiplication tensors

We will define the polynomial multiplication tensors and show that, over every field, P_<sub>a,b</sub>_ has border rank at most _a+b_-1 and P_<sub>n,n</sub>_ degenerates to \(\langle n\rangle\).

**Definition 3.1.** For integers \(a,b\ge 1\), the _polynomial multiplication tensor_ is<tbc>

\(\mathsf{P}_{a,b}:=\sum_{i=1}^a\sum_{j=1}^be_i\otimes e_j\otimes e_{i+j-1}\in\mathbb{F}^a\otimes\mathbb{F}^b\otimes\mathbb{F}^{a+b-1}.\)

<tbc>The tensor P_<sub>a,b</sub>_ corresponds to the multiplication of a polynomial of degree at most _a_-1 by a polynomial of degree at most _b_-1: if _e<sub>i</sub>_ stands for the monomial _t_<sup>_i_-1</sup> in an indeterminate _t_, then the term \(e_i\otimes e_j\otimes e_{i+j-1}\) of P_<sub>a,b</sub>_ records the product _t_<sup>_i_-1</sup>_t_<sup>_j_-1</sup>=_t_<sup>_i+j_-2</sup>. For an integer \(d\ge 0\), let \(\mathbb{F}[t]_{\le d}\) be the space of polynomials of degree at most _d_ in _t_. In this way the tensor P_<sub>a,b</sub>_ corresponds to the bilinear multiplication map

\(\mathbb{F}[t]_{\le a-1}\times\mathbb{F}[t]_{\le b-1}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}[t]_{\le a+b-2}:(f,g)\mapstofg.\) (3.1)

For _a_=1, \(\mathsf{P}_{1,b}=\sum_{j=1}^be_1\otimes e_j\otimes e_j\) is isomorphic to \(\langle 1,1,b\rangle=\sum_{k=1}^bE_{11}\otimes E_{1k}\otimes E_{k1}\): it describes the multiplication of a polynomial of degree at most _b_-1 by a constant, which is nothing else than multiplying a vector of length _b_ by a constant.

**Proposition 3.2.** _Let_ \(a,b\ge 1\) _be integers. Then_ \(\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\triangleleft\langle a+b-1\rangle\).

_Proof._ We extend the field by a formal variable _z_ and consider the function field F(_z_). The field F(_z_) is infinite so \(\mathsf{R}_{\mathbb{F}(z)}(\mathsf{P}_{a,b})\le a+b-1\) \[BCS97, Proposition 14.47\], that is, \(\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\le\langle a+b-1\rangle\) as tensors over F(_z_) (Lemma 2.1(ii)). A restriction over F(_z_) is a degeneration over F (Lemma 2.2(iv)), which proves the claim.

**Lemma 3.3** (\[BCS97, Proposition 14.48(1)\])**.** _For every integer_ \(n\ge 1\)_, we have_ \(\langle n\rangle\triangleleft\mathsf{P}_{n,n}\).

_Proof._ If F has at least _n_ elements, the cited proposition gives \(\langle n\rangle\le\mathsf{P}_{n,n}\): for a product _f_ of _n_ distinct linear factors, the multiplication tensor of the algebra \(\mathbb{F}[t]/(f)\cong\mathbb{F}^n\) is \(\langle n\rangle\). Over every field, we apply Lemma 2.6 to _S_=P_<sub>n,n</sub>_, with the weights _w_<sub>1</sub>(_i_)=2(_i_-1)<sup>2</sup>, _w_<sub>2</sub>(_j_)=2(_j_-1)<sup>2</sup> and _w_<sub>3</sub>(_k_)=-(_k_-1)<sup>2</sup>. The term \(e_i\otimes e_j\otimes e_{i+j-1}\) of P_<sub>n,n</sub>_ has weight 2(_i_-1)<sup>2</sup>+2(_j_-1)<sup>2</sup>-(_i+j_-2)<sup>2</sup>=(_i-j_)<sup>2</sup>\(\ge 0\), which is 0 exactly when _i=j_. So \(\mathsf{P}_{n,n}\unknown\sum_{i=1}^ne_i\otimes e_i\otimes e_{2i-1}\). The linear map on the third leg that maps _e_<sub>2_i_-1</sub> to _e<sub>i</sub>_ for every \(i\in[n]\) and the other basis vectors to 0 maps this tensor to \(\langle n\rangle\), so \(\langle n\rangle\triangleleft\mathsf{P}_{n,n}\).

## 3.2 Separating partial direct sums into direct sums

In this subsection we will prove a separation lemma that degenerates any partial direct sum (Section 2.1) to a direct sum, in the presence of a polynomial multiplication tensor factor.

A degeneration on the second and third legs (Section 2.4) can be applied to some of the summands of a partial direct sum, while the other summands stay as they are: if \(T\triangleleft_1S\), then \(T\oplus_1C\triangleleft_1S\oplus_1C\) for every tensor _C_ with the same first leg as _S_ and _T_. If \((I\otimes A_2\otimes A_3)S=\varepsilon^qT+\varepsilon^{q+1}T_1+\cdots+\varepsilon^{q+d}T_d\), then \(I\otimes(A_2\oplus\varepsilon^qI)\otimes(A_3\oplus I)\) maps \(S\oplus_1C\) to \(\varepsilon^q(T\oplus_1C)+\varepsilon^{q+1}T_1+\cdots+\varepsilon^{q+d}T_d\).

**Lemma 3.4.** _Let_ \(T\in U\otimes V\otimes W\) _be a tensor and let_ \(k\ge 1\) _be an integer. Then the partial direct sum_ \(T\oplus_1\cdots\oplus_1T\) _of k copies of T is isomorphic to_ \(T\otimes\langle 1,1,k\rangle\).

_Proof._ We have \(\langle 1,1,k\rangle=\sum_{\ell=1}^kE_{11}\otimes E_{1\ell}\otimes E_{\ell 1}\). So \(T\otimes\langle 1,1,k\rangle\) is a partial direct sum of _k_ copies of _T_, the \(\ell\)th in \((U\otimes\mathbb{F}^{1\times 1})\otimes(V\otimes\mathbb{F}E_{1\ell})\otimes(W\otimes\mathbb{F}E_{\ell 1})\).

**Proposition 3.5** (From partial direct sum to direct sum)**.** _Let_ \(m,t\ge 1\) _be integers. Let T_<sub>1</sub>_,...,T<sub>m</sub> be tensors with_ \(T_\ell\in U\otimes V_\ell\otimes W_\ell\)_. Then_

\((T_1\oplus\cdots\oplus T_m)\otimes\mathsf{P}_{1,t}\triangleleft(T_1\oplus_1\cdots\oplus_1T_m)\otimes\mathsf{P}_{m,t}.\)

Note how in the degeneration of Proposition 3.5, the right-hand side has the polynomial multiplication tensor P_<sub>m,t</sub>_ as a factor, and the left-hand side the polynomial multiplication tensor P<sub>1_,t_</sub>. We may think of P_<sub>m,t</sub>_ as a resource that enables the degeneration while being partially "consumed" in the process, leaving P<sub>1_,t_</sub> in the result.

_Proof._ Let \(T=T_1\oplus_1\cdots\oplus_1T_m\). Without loss of generality (embed the spaces into F_<sup>n</sup>_ for a large enough _n_, which gives restrictions in both directions), we take \(U=V_\ell=W_\ell=\mathbb{F}^n\). Let \(\{e_a\}_a\), \(\{e_b^\ell\}_b\) and \(\{e_c^\ell\}_c\) be the standard bases for _U_, \(V_\ell\) and \(W_\ell\) respectively. By definition,

\(T\otimes\mathsf{P}_{m,t}=\sum_{\ell=1}^m\sum_{a,b,c=1}^n\sum_{i\in[m],j\in[t]}(T_\ell)_{a,b,c}\left(e_a\otimes e_i\right)\otimes\left(e_b^\ell\otimes e_j\right)\otimes\left(e_c^\ell\otimes e_{i+j-1}\right).\) (3.2)

We will apply a monomial degeneration, as in Lemma 2.6, to this tensor. Define the weights<tbc>

\(w_1(e_a\otimes e_i)=i^2,w_2(e_b^\ell\otimes e_j)=\ell^2+2\ell(j-1),w_3(e_c^\ell\otimes e_k)=-2\ell k.\)

<tbc>On the term with indices \(\ell\), _i_ and _j_, the third-leg index is _k=i+j_-1, and the sum of the weights is \(i^2+\ell^2+2\ell(j-1)-2\ell(i+j-1)=(i-\ell)^2\). This is nonnegative, and zero exactly when \(i=\ell\). So \(T\otimes\mathsf{P}_{m,t}\) degenerates to

\(\sum_{\ell=1}^m\sum_{a,b,c}\sum_{j\in[t]}(T_\ell)_{a,b,c}\left(e_a\otimes e_\ell\right)\otimes(e_b^\ell\otimes e_j)\otimes(e_c^\ell\otimes e_{\ell+j-1}).\)

The \(\ell\)th summand lies in \((U\otimes e_\ell)\otimes(V_\ell\otimes\mathbb{F}^t)\otimes(W_\ell\otimes\mathbb{F}^{m+t-1})\), so the summands no longer share the first leg. Mapping \(e_c^\ell\otimes e_{\ell+j-1}\) to \(e_c^\ell\otimes e_j\), and all other basis vectors to 0, on the third leg restricts this tensor to \((T_1\otimes\mathsf{P}_{1,t})\oplus\cdots\oplus(T_m\otimes\mathsf{P}_{1,t})=(T_1\oplus\cdots\oplus T_m)\otimes\mathsf{P}_{1,t}\).

## 3.3 Concavity degeneration for P_<sub>a,b</sub>_

In this subsection we will prove a degeneration relation among polynomial multiplication tensors P_<sub>a,b</sub>_, which can be interpreted as a discrete concavity in _b_. We will first prove it using Lemma 2.5. Afterwards, we will give a second proof over C, using the Clebsch-Gordan rule for representations of the special linear group SL<sub>2</sub>(C).

**Lemma 3.6** (Concavity degeneration)**.** _Let_ \(a\ge 1\) _and_ \(b\ge 2\) _be integers. Then_<tbc>

\(\mathsf{P}_{a,b+1}\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{a,b-1}\triangle_1\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{a,b}.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ We will apply Lemma 2.5 to the bilinear map that sends (_f,(g,h_)) to (_fg,fh_), whose tensor is \(\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\), and to subspaces for which the induced maps on the subspaces and on the quotients have tensors P_<sub>a,b</sub>_-1 and P_<sub>a,b</sub>_+1. For every integer \(d\ge 0\), let \(\mathcal{W}_d:=\mathbb{F}[t]_{\le d}\). For every integer \(d\ge 2\), let<tbc>

\(\iota_d:\mathcal{W}_{d-2}\rightarrow\mathcal{W}_{d-1}\oplus\mathcal{W}_{d-1}:p\mapsto(-tp,p),\sigma_d:\mathcal{W}_{d-1}\oplus\mathcal{W}_{d-1}\rightarrow\mathcal{W}_d:(g,h)\mapsto g+th.\)

<tbc>Then \(\iota_d\) is injective and \(\sigma_d\) is surjective. For \(g,h\in\mathcal{W}_{d-1}\), we have _g+th_=0 exactly when _g_=-_th_ and \(h\in\mathcal{W}_{d-2}\), so the kernel of \(\sigma_d\) is the image of \(\iota_d\). Let \(V:=\mathcal{W}_{b-1}\oplus\mathcal{W}_{b-1}\) and \(W:=\mathcal{W}_{a+b-2}\oplus\mathcal{W}_{a+b-2}\), and consider the bilinear map<tbc>

\(\mu:\mathcal{W}_{a-1}\times V\rightarrow W:\left(f,(g,h)\right)\mapsto(fg,fh),\)

whose tensor _T_ is \(\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\). Let _V_<sub>1</sub> be the image of \(\iota_b\) and _W_<sub>1</sub> the image of \(\iota_{a+b-1}\). We claim<tbc>

\(\mu(\mathcal{W}_{a-1}\times V_1)\subseteq W_1.\)

<tbc>This claim will let us apply Lemma 2.5. Indeed, for all \(f\in\mathcal{W}_{a-1}\) and \(p\in\mathcal{W}_{b-2}\),<tbc>

\(\mu\big(f,\iota_b(p)\big)=(-tfp,fp)=\iota_{a+b-1}(fp).\) (3.3)

<tbc>By Lemma 2.5, \(T\unknown_1T_1\oplus_1T_2\) for the tensors _T_<sub>1</sub> and _T_<sub>2</sub> of the bilinear maps

\(\mu_1:\mathcal{W}_{a-1}\times(V/V_1)\rightarrow(W/W_1)\text{and}\mu_2:\mathcal{W}_{a-1}\times V_1\rightarrow W_1\)

induced by \(\mu\). It remains to show that \(T_1\cong\mathsf{P}_{a,b+1}\) and \(T_2\cong\mathsf{P}_{a,b-1}\).

For _T_<sub>2</sub> this follows from (3.3), where we identify \(\mathcal{W}_{b-2}\cong V_1\) using the isomorphism \(\iota_b:\mathcal{W}_{b-2}\rightarrow V_1\), and similarly \(\mathcal{W}_{a+b-3}\cong W_1\).

For _T_<sub>1</sub> we use that the maps \(\sigma_b\) and \(\sigma_{a+b-1}\) are surjective with kernels _V_<sub>1</sub> and _W_<sub>1</sub>, so they induce isomorphisms from the quotients to W_<sub>b</sub>_ and W<sub>_a+b_-1</sub>. Since

\(\sigma_{a+b-1}\big(\mu(f,(g,h))\big)=fg+tfh=f\sigma_b(g,h)\)

for all \(f\in\mathcal{W}_{a-1}\) and \(g,h\in\mathcal{W}_{b-1}\), these isomorphisms identify the induced map \(\mu_1\) on the quotients with the multiplication map \(\mathcal{W}_{a-1}\times\mathcal{W}_b\rightarrow\mathcal{W}_{a+b-1}\), whose tensor is P<sub>_a,b_+1</sub>.

We now give the second proof, over C, which is insightful for readers familiar with representation theory. For \(d\ge 1\) let \(\mathcal{V}_d:=\mathrm{Sym}^d\mathbb{C}^2\subseteq(\mathbb{C}^2)^{\otimes d}\) be the subspace of symmetric tensors of order _d_ and let V<sub>0</sub>:=C. Then V_<sub>d</sub>_ is an irreducible SL<sub>2</sub>(C) representation under the diagonal action \(g\mapsto g^{\otimes d}\) of SL<sub>2</sub>(C), and its dual \(\mathcal{V}_d^*\) is isomorphic to the space C\[_x,y_\]_<sub>d</sub>_ of homogeneous polynomials of degree _d_ as an SL<sub>2</sub>(C) representation (see Fulton and Harris \[FH91, Chapter 11\]). We can identify \(\mathbb{C}[t]_{\le d}\) with C\[_x,y_\]_<sub>d</sub>_ via homogenization \(t^k\mapsto x^ky^{d-k}\). Under this identification, the polynomial multiplication tensor P<sub>_a,b_</sub> by definition describes the (bilinear) multiplication map \(\mathbb{C}[x,y]_{a-1}\times\mathbb{C}[x,y]_{b-1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}[x,y]_{a+b-2}\). This map is SL<sub>2</sub>(C) equivariant. Under the standard identification of bilinear maps with tensors we have that \(\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\in\mathcal{V}_{a-1}\otimes\mathcal{V}_{b-1}\otimes\mathcal{V}_{a+b-2}^*\). Because this identification is SL<sub>2</sub>(C) equivariant, we obtain that P<sub>_a,b_</sub> is invariant under the diagonal SL<sub>2</sub>(C) action, that is, \(\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\in(\mathcal{V}_{a-1}\otimes\mathcal{V}_{b-1}\otimes\mathcal{V}_{a+b-2}^*)^{\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})}\).

**Lemma 3.7.** _Let_ \(i,j\ge 0\) _be integers. We have that_ \(\mathcal{V}_i\otimes\mathcal{V}_j\cong\oplus_{k=0}^{\mathrm{min}(i,j)}\mathcal{V}_{i+j-2k}\)_. In particular, for every integer_ \(\ell>i+j\), \((\mathcal{V}_i\otimes\mathcal{V}_j\otimes\mathcal{V}_\ell^*)^{\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})}=0\) _and_ \((\mathcal{V}_i\otimes\mathcal{V}_j\otimes\mathcal{V}_{i+j}^*)^{\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})}=\mathbb{C}\mathsf{P}_{i+1,j+1}\).

_Proof._ The first statement is standard, see e.g. \[FH91, Exercise 11.11\]. ## 4.1 Spectral points, asymptotic spectrum duality, and basic properties

In this subsection we will define Strassen’s asymptotic spectrum, whose elements are called spectral points, and state the properties that we will use, including the asymptotic spectrum duality theorem. Strassen introduced these to study the asymptotic restriction of tensors, and in particular the exponent of matrix multiplication \[Str88\]. For background, see the survey of Wigderson and Zuiddam \[WZ26\].

**Definition 4.1** (Strassen \[Str88, Section 3\])**.** A _spectral point_ is a map \(\phi:\mathcal{S}_\mathbb{F}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) such that \(\phi(\langle 1\rangle)=1\) and, for all tensors _S_ and _T_ over F, we have \(\phi(S\oplus T)=\phi(S)+\phi(T)\) and \(\phi(S\otimes T)=\phi(S)\phi(T)\), and if \(T\le S\), then \(\phi(T)\le\phi(S)\). The _asymptotic spectrum_ of tensors over F is the set \(\Delta_\mathbb{F}\) of spectral points.

For the upper bounds on \(\omega_\mathbb{F}\) and \(\omega_\mathbb{F}(a,b,c)\), we will not need to know what the spectral points are beyond their abstract definition! Spectral points have been constructed explicitly, but it is not known whether these constructions give all of the asymptotic spectrum \[Str91, CVZ23, SDW26\].

The simplest spectral points are the flattening ranks R<sub>(1)</sub>, R<sub>(2)</sub> and R<sub>(3)</sub> of Section 2.2, since the rank of matrices is normalised, additive, multiplicative and monotone under restriction. They are the only explicit spectral points that we will use, in examples and to show that some of the bounds are attained.

From the definition it readily follows that spectral points lower bound the matrix multiplication exponent: for every \(\phi\in\Delta_\mathbb{F}\) we have \(log\phi(\langle 2,2,2\rangle)\le\omega_\mathbb{F}\). Strassen proved that these spectral point lower bounds are complete:

**Theorem 4.2** (Strassen \[Str88, Theorem 3.8 and Proposition 4.2\])**.** _We have_

\(max_{\phi\in\Delta_\mathbb{F}}log\phi(\langle 2,2,2\rangle)=\omega_\mathbb{F}.\)

To upper bound \(\omega_\mathbb{F}\) it thus suffices to upper bound \(\phi(\langle 2,2,2\rangle)\) for every \(\phi\in\Delta_\mathbb{F}\). This we will do by taking the degenerations constructed in Section 3, applying the spectral points to them, and optimising over these inequalities to upper bound the value of \(\phi(\langle 2,2,2\rangle)\). In Section 5 we will show that no combination of these degenerations by the combination rules gives a better bound.

The values of a spectral point \(\phi\) at the tensors \(\langle 1,1,2\rangle\), \(\langle 2,1,1\rangle\) and \(\langle 1,2,1\rangle\) will play a central role. The following are the basic properties of spectral points that we will need. For a given \(\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3\), we define the permutation \(\phi_\pi\) of \(\phi\) as

\(\phi_\pi(T):=\phi(\pi\cdot T).\) (4.1)

**Lemma 4.3** (Strassen \[Str87, Proposition 5.10\], \[Str88, Theorem 3.1 and Proposition 4.3\])**.** _Let_ \(\phi\in\Delta_\mathbb{F}\).

(i) _For all tensors S and T over_ F _with_ \(T\triangleleft S\)_, we have_ \(\phi(T)\le\phi(S)\).<tbc>

(ii) _For every integer_ \(n\ge 0\)_, we have_ \(\phi(\langle n\rangle)=n\).<tbc>

(iii) _For every nonzero tensor T over_ F_, we have_ \(\phi(T)\ge 1\).<tbc>

(iv) _The values_ \(\phi(\langle 1,1,2\rangle)\), \(\phi(\langle 2,1,1\rangle)\) _and_ \(\phi(\langle 1,2,1\rangle)\) _lie in the interval_ \[1,2\]_, and for all integers_ \(n_1,n_2,n_3\ge 1\),<tbc>

<tbc>\(\phi(\langle n_1,n_2,n_3\rangle)=\phi(\langle 2,1,1\rangle)^{logn_1}\phi(\langle 1,2,1\rangle)^{logn_2}\phi(\langle 1,1,2\rangle)^{logn_3}.\)<tbc>

<tbc>_In particular,_ \(\phi(\langle m,m,m\rangle)=\phi(\langle 2,2,2\rangle)^{logn}\) _for every integer_ \(m\ge 1\).<tbc>

(v) \(\phi_\pi\in\Delta_\mathbb{F}\).

_Proof._ Part (i) is \[Str87, Proposition 5.10\] and \[Str88, Theorem 3.1\]. Part (ii) holds since \(\langle n\rangle\) is the direct sum of _n_ copies of \(\langle 1\rangle\), and part (iii) follows since \(\langle 1\rangle\le T\) for every nonzero tensor _T_ (Lemma 2.1(i)). The formula in part (iv) is \[Str88, Proposition 4.3\]. The bounds on the three values follow from parts (i)-(iii), since each of the tensors \(\langle 1,1,2\rangle\), \(\langle 2,1,1\rangle\) and \(\langle 1,2,1\rangle\) is nonzero and a restriction of \(\langle 2\rangle\). Part (v) follows since permuting the legs of a tensor commutes with direct sums and tensor products, fixes \(\langle 1\rangle\) and preserves restriction (Lemma 2.1(iv)).

Strassen also expressed the exponents of rectangular matrix multiplication as a maximum over spectral points.

**Lemma 4.4** (Strassen \[Str88, Proposition 4.5\])**.** _Let_ \(a,b,c\ge 0\) _be real numbers. Then_

\(2^{\omega_\mathbb{F}(a,b,c)}=\mathrm{max}_{\phi\in\Delta_\mathbb{F}}\phi(\langle 2,1,1\rangle)^a\phi(\langle 1,2,1\rangle)^b\phi(\langle 1,1,2\rangle)^c.\)

## 4.2 Superadditivity on partial direct sums

In this subsection we will show that, for every \(\phi\in\Delta_\mathbb{F}\) with \(p:=\mathrm{log}\phi(\langle 1,1,2\rangle)>0\), the function \(\phi^{1/p}\) is superadditive on partial direct sums (Lemma 4.6). We will first treat isomorphic summands using Proposition 3.5 (Lemma 4.5), and then remove the hypothesis that the summands are isomorphic by applying this case to tensor powers. As a first application, we will obtain \(\omega_\mathbb{F}<2.3212\) from a tensor of Strassen (Proposition 4.8).

Let_ \(r\ge 1\) _be an integer, and let_ \(S=S_1\oplus_1\cdots\oplus_1S_r\) _be a partial direct sum in which each S<sub>i</sub> is isomorphic to S_<sub>1</sub>_. Then_<tbc>

\(\phi(S)\ge\frac{1}{2}r^p\phi(S_1).\)

<tbc>_Proof._ We have<tbc>

\((S_1\oplus\cdots\oplus S_r)\otimes\mathsf{P}_{1,r}\unknown S\otimes\mathsf{P}_{r,r}\unknown S\otimes\langle 2r-1\rangle.\)

<tbc>The first degeneration is Proposition 3.5 with _m=t=r_. The second follows by tensoring the border rank bound \(\mathsf{P}_{r,r}\unknown\langle 2r-1\rangle\) (Proposition 3.2) with _S_. The left-hand side is isomorphic to \(\langle r\rangle\otimes S_1\otimes\langle 1,1,r\rangle\), since \(S_1\oplus\cdots\oplus S_r\cong\langle r\rangle\otimes S_1\) and \(\mathsf{P}_{1,r}\cong\langle 1,1,r\rangle\). The spectral point \(\phi\) is multiplicative and monotone under degeneration, \(\phi(\langle n\rangle)=n\) for every integer \(n\ge 1\), and \(\phi(\langle 1,1,r\rangle)=r^p\) (Lemma 4.3(i), (ii) and (iv)). So

\(r^{1+p}\phi(S_1)\le(2r-1)\phi(S).\)

Since \(r/(2r-1)\ge 1/2\), it follows that \(\phi(S)\ge\frac{1}{2}r^p\phi(S_1)\).

**Lemma 4.6** (Superadditivity)**.** _Let_ \(\phi\in\Delta_\mathbb{F}\)_, and suppose that_ \(p:=\mathrm{log}\phi(\langle 1,1,2\rangle)\) _is positive. Let_ \(m\ge 1\) _be an integer. For_ \(\ell\in[m]\)_, let_ \(T_\ell\in U\otimes V_\ell\otimes W_\ell\) _be tensors over_ F_. Then_<tbc>

\(\phi(T_1\oplus_1\cdots\oplus_1T_m)^{1/p}\ge\phi(T_1)^{1/p}+\cdots+\phi(T_m)^{1/p}.\)

We recover Proposition 4.8 by setting \(S=\langle q,1,1\rangle\) and _s=t_=1, and applying \(\mathrm{Str}_q\unknown\langle q+1\rangle\).

**Lemma 4.9** (Symmetrised partial direct sums)**.** _Let S be a tensor over_ F_, and let_ \(s,t\ge 1\) _be integers. Then_<tbc>

\(\otimes_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3}\pi\cdot\big(S\otimes\langle 1,1,s+t\rangle\big)\lesssim\otimes_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3}\pi\cdot\big(\big(S\otimes\langle 1,1,s\rangle\big)\oplus_1\big(((23)\cdot S)\otimes\langle 1,1,t\rangle\big)\big).\)

<tbc>_Proof._ Let \(T:=(S\otimes\langle 1,1,s\rangle)\oplus_1(((23)\cdot S)\otimes\langle 1,1,t\rangle)\), and let \(\phi\in\Delta_\mathbb{F}\). By Strassen’s duality theorem \[Str88, Theorem 3.2\], and since \(\phi\) is multiplicative and the six permutations form three pairs \(\{\pi,\pi\circ(23)\}\), it suffices to show that<tbc>

\(\phi_\pi(T)\phi_{\pi\circ(23)}(T)\ge\phi_\pi\big(S\otimes\langle 1,1,s+t\rangle\big)\phi_{\pi\circ(23)}\big(S\otimes\langle 1,1,s+t\rangle\big)\)

<tbc>for every \(\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3\). Fix \(\pi\), and let \(p:=\mathrm{log}\phi_\pi(\langle 1,1,2\rangle)\), \(x:=\phi_\pi(S)\) and \(y:=\phi_{\pi\circ(23)}(S)\). Since \((23)\cdot\langle 1,1,2\rangle\cong\langle 1,1,2\rangle\), also \(\phi_{\pi\circ(23)}(\langle 1,1,2\rangle)=2^p\), so \(\phi_\pi(\langle 1,1,m\rangle)=\phi_{\pi\circ(23)}(\langle 1,1,m\rangle)=m^p\) for every integer \(m\ge 1\) (Lemma 4.3(iv) and (v)). So the right-hand side is (_s+t_)<sup>2_p_</sup>_xy_. Moreover, \(\phi_\pi((23)\cdot S)=y\) and \(\phi_{\pi\circ(23)}((23)\cdot S)=x\). If _p\>_0, then Lemma 4.6 for \(\phi_\pi\) and for \(\phi_{\pi\circ(23)}\) gives

\(\phi_\pi(T)^{1/p}\ge sx^{1/p}+ty^{1/p}\text{and}\phi_{\pi\circ(23)}(T)^{1/p}\ge sy^{1/p}+tx^{1/p},\)

and \((sx^{1/p}+ty^{1/p})(sy^{1/p}+tx^{1/p})\ge(s+t)^2(xy)^{1/p}\), since the difference is _st(x_<sup>1_/p_</sup>-_y_<sup>1_/p_</sup>)<sup>2</sup>. Raising to the power _p_ gives the claim. If _p_=0, then the restriction \(T\ge S\otimes\langle 1,1,s\rangle\) gives \(\phi_\pi(T)\ge x\) and \(\phi_{\pi\circ(23)}(T)\ge y\), which is the claim.

## 4.3 Concavity and tripling for each leg

In this subsection we will bound the values \(\phi(\mathsf{P}_{a,b})\) of a spectral point \(\phi\) at the polynomial multiplication tensors. We will show that, if \(p:=\mathrm{log}\phi(\langle 1,1,2\rangle)>0\), then \(b\mapsto\phi(\mathsf{P}_{a,b})^{1/p}\) is concave and satisfies a tripling inequality (Lemma 4.10). The results follows directly from the degenerations of Section 3, combined with Lemma 4.6, see  1.

We call a function \(h:\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) _concave_ if \(h(m+1)+h(m-1)\le 2h(m)\) for every \(m\ge 2\).

**Lemma 4.10.** _Let_ \(\phi\in\Delta_\mathbb{F}\)_, and let_ \(p:=log\phi(\langle 1,1,2\rangle)\).

(i) _For all_ \(a,b\ge 1\)_, we have_ \(min(a,b)\le\phi(\mathsf{P}_{a,b})\le a+b-1\)_, and_ \(\phi(\mathsf{P}_{a,b})\) _is nondecreasing in a and in b._<tbc>

(ii) _If p\>_0_, then for all_ \(a\ge 1\)_, the function_ \(b\mapsto\phi(\mathsf{P}_{a,b})^{1/p}\) _is concave._<tbc>

(iii) _If p\>_0_, then for all_ \(a,b\ge 1\)_, we have_ \(2\phi(\mathsf{P}_{a,b})^{1/p}+\phi((23)\cdot\mathsf{P}_{a,b})^{1/p}\le\phi(\mathsf{P}_{a,3b+a-1})^{1/p}\).

_Proof._ (i) For _n_=min(_a,b_), the degenerations \(\langle n\rangle\triangleleft\mathsf{P}_{n,n}\le\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\) (Lemma 3.3) give \(n=\phi(\langle n\rangle)\le\phi(\mathsf{P}_{a,b})\) (Lemma 4.3(i) and (ii)), and \(\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\triangleleft\langle a+b-1\rangle\) (Proposition 3.2) gives \(\phi(\mathsf{P}_{a,b})\le a+b-1\). If \(a_1\le a_2\) and \(b_1\le b_2\), then \(\mathsf{P}_{a_1,b_1}\le\mathsf{P}_{a_2,b_2}\), so \(\phi(\mathsf{P}_{a_1,b_1})\le\phi(\mathsf{P}_{a_2,b_2})\).

(ii) and (iii) Suppose that _p\>_0. By Lemma 3.6 and Lemma 3.4, for all integers \(a\ge 1\) and \(b\ge 2\),<tbc>

\(\mathsf{P}_{a,b+1}\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{a,b-1}\triangleleft\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\otimes\langle 1,1,2\rangle,\)

<tbc>and by Lemma 3.11, for all integers \(a,b\ge 1\),

\(\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\oplus_1((23)\cdot\mathsf{P}_{a,b})\oplus_1\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\triangleleft\mathsf{P}_{a,3b+a-1}.\)

Moreover, \(\phi(\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\otimes\langle 1,1,2\rangle)=2^p\phi(\mathsf{P}_{a,b})\). So Lemma 4.6 and the monotonicity of \(\phi\) under degeneration give (ii) from the first degeneration and (iii) from the second.

In the subsequent sections we will use the following definition as a shorthand:

\(\phi(a,b):=\phi(\mathsf{P}_{a,b}).\) (4.2)

## 4.4 Square matrix multiplication

In this subsection we will prove Theorem 1.1. By Theorem 4.2, it suffices to show that \(\phi(\langle 2,2,2\rangle)\le 2^{9/4}\) for every \(\phi\in\Delta_\mathbb{F}\). For this we will use Lemma 4.10 applied to \(\phi_\pi\) with \(\pi\) ranging over S<sub>3</sub>. In the case that \(p:=log\phi_\pi(\langle 1,1,2\rangle)>0\), we will apply Lemma 4.11 to the functions \(b\mapsto\phi_\pi(a,b)^{1/p}\) and \(b\mapsto\phi_{\pi\circ(23)}(a,b)^{1/p}\) appearing in Lemma 4.10. Roughly speaking, this will then allow us to lower bound the growth of \(n\mapsto\phi_\pi(n,n)\) in terms of _p_. Subsequently, we will obtain a lower bound on \(\phi\) evaluated on \(\otimes_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3}\pi\cdot\mathsf{P}_{n,n}\) in terms of \(\phi(\langle 2,2,2\rangle)\). The upper bound will then follow from the fact that \(\otimes_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3}\pi\cdot\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\) has low border rank (Proposition 3.2).

In Sections 4.5 and 4.6 we will treat the rectangular case. Those sections will not rely on any result from this section, and the results there will also recover the results of this section. So, this section can also safely be skipped.

We begin with a general lemma about concave functions.

**Lemma 4.11.** _Let_ \(a\ge 1\) _be an integer, and let_ \(g,h:\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{>0}\) _be concave functions such that_ \(2g(m)+h(m)\le g(3m+a-1)\) _and_ \(2h(m)+g(m)\le h(3m+a-1)\) _for every integer_ \(m\ge 1\)_. Then for every integer_ \(b\ge 1\),<tbc>

\(\frac{g(b+1)}{g(b)}\frac{h(b+1)}{h(b)}\ge\big(\frac{2b+a+1}{2b+a-1}\big)^2.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ Let _D_=2_b+a_-1 and _S=g(b_)+_h(b_). Since _g_ is concave, its differences _g(k_+1)-_g(k_) do not increase with _k_. So _g(b_+1)-_g(b_) is at least the average of the _D_ differences _g(j_+1)-_g(j_) with \(b\le j<3b+a-1\), and the first hypothesis with _m=b_ gives<tbc>

\(g(b+1)-g(b)\ge\frac{g(3b+a-1)-g(b)}{D}\ge\frac{S}{D}.\)

<tbc>Likewise, the second hypothesis gives \(h(b+1)-h(b)\ge S/D\). Since \(S^2\ge 4g(b)h(b)\), we find<tbc>

\(g(b+1)h(b+1)\ge\big(g(b)+\frac{S}{D}\big)\big(h(b)+\frac{S}{D}\big)=g(b)h(b)+\frac{S^2}{D}+\frac{S^2}{D^2}\ge g(b)h(b)\big(1+\frac{2}{D}\big)^2.\)

<tbc>**Proposition 4.12.** _Let_ \(\phi\in\Delta_\mathbb{F}\)_, and let_ \(\tau:=log\phi(\langle 2,2,2\rangle)\)_. Then for every integer_ \(n\ge 1\),<tbc>

\(\prod_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3}\phi(\pi\cdot\mathsf{P}_{n,n})\ge\big(\frac{3n-1}{2}\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\frac{3k+1}{3k}\big)^{2\tau}\ge n^{8\tau/3}.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ Let _p_<sub>1</sub>, _p_<sub>2</sub> and _p_<sub>3</sub> be the logarithms of \(\phi(\langle 1,1,2\rangle)\), \(\phi(\langle 2,1,1\rangle)\) and \(\phi(\langle 1,2,1\rangle)\), so that \(\tau=p_1+p_2+p_3\) (Lemma 4.3(iv)). For every integer \(n\ge 1\), let \(G_n:=\prod_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3}\phi_\pi(n,n)\), the left-hand side of the claim. Since \(\phi_\pi(1,1)=1\) (Lemma 4.10(i) for \(\phi_\pi\)), we have _G_<sub>1</sub>=1. Now fix an integer \(n\ge 1\), and let \(\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3\). Using that \(\phi_\pi(n+1,n)=\phi_{\pi\circ(12)}(n,n+1)\) and \(\phi_\pi(n,n)=\phi_{\pi\circ(12)}(n,n)\), since \(\phi_\pi(a,b)=\phi_{\pi\circ(12)}(b,a)\), we obtain<tbc>

\(\frac{\phi_\pi(n+1,n+1)}{\phi_\pi(n,n)}=\frac{\phi_\pi(n+1,n+1)}{\phi_\pi(n+1,n)}\cdot\frac{\phi_{\pi\circ(12)}(n,n+1)}{\phi_{\pi\circ(12)}(n,n)}.\)

<tbc>We multiply over \(\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3\). Since \(\pi\mapsto\pi\circ(12)\) is a bijection of S<sub>3</sub>, this gives<tbc>

\(\frac{G_{n+1}}{G_n}=\prod_{a\in\{n,n+1\}}\prod_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_3}\frac{\phi_\sigma(a,n+1)}{\phi_\sigma(a,n)}.\)

<tbc>The six permutations form three pairs \(\{\sigma,\sigma\circ(23)\}\), one for each \(i\in\{1,2,3\}\), with \(\sigma(1)=i\). Let \(a\in\{n,n+1\}\). If _p<sub>i</sub>\>_0, then by Lemma 4.10, applied to \(\phi_\sigma\) and \(\phi_{\sigma\circ(23)}\), the functions \(m\mapsto\phi_\sigma(a,m)^{1/p_i}\) and \(m\mapsto\phi_{\sigma\circ(23)}(a,m)^{1/p_i}\) satisfy the hypotheses of Lemma 4.11. Here we use that both spectral points take the value 2_<sup>p<sub>i</sub></sup>_ at \(\langle 1,1,2\rangle\), since \(\sigma\) and \(\sigma\circ(23)\) move its one- dimensional first leg to leg _i_, and that \(\phi_\sigma((23)\cdot T)=\phi_{\sigma\circ(23)}(T)\) and \(\phi_{\sigma\circ(23)}((23)\cdot T)=\phi_\sigma(T)\) for every tensor _T_, since \(\pi\cdot(\rho\cdot T)=(\pi\circ\rho)\cdot T\) for all \(\pi,\rho\in\mathfrak{S}_3\). That lemma with _b=n_, raised to the power _p<sub>i</sub>_, gives<tbc>

\(\frac{\phi_\sigma(a,n+1)}{\phi_\sigma(a,n)}\cdot\frac{\phi_{\sigma\circ(23)}(a,n+1)}{\phi_{\sigma\circ(23)}(a,n)}\ge\big(\frac{2n+a+1}{2n+a-1}\big)^{2p_i}.\)

<tbc>If _p<sub>i</sub>_=0, this holds as well, since the left-hand side is at least 1: \(\phi_\sigma\) and \(\phi_{\sigma\circ(23)}\) are nondecreasing in the second argument (Lemma 4.10(i)). Multiplying over the three pairs and the two values of _a_ gives<tbc>

\(\frac{G_{n+1}}{G_n}\ge\big(\frac{(3n+1)(3n+2)}{(3n-1)3n}\big)^{2\tau},\text{so}G_n\ge\big(\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\frac{(3k+1)(3k+2)}{(3k-1)3k}\big)^{2\tau},\)

where we multiply these inequalities and use that _G_<sub>1</sub>=1. The factors (3_k_+2)/(3_k_-1) telescope to (3_n_-1)/2, which gives the first inequality of the claim. For the second, we use that \(\tau\ge 0\), \((3n-1)/2\ge n\), and \((3k+1)/(3k)\ge((k+1)/k)^{1/3}\) by the binomial theorem, so that \(\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}(3k+1)/(3k)\ge n^{1/3}\).

_Proof of Theorem 1.1._ Let \(\phi\in\Delta_\mathbb{F}\), and let \(\tau:=\mathrm{log}\phi(\langle 2,2,2\rangle)\). Since \(\phi(\pi\cdot\mathsf{P}_{n,n})\le 2n-1\) for every \(\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3\) (Lemma 4.10(i) for \(\phi_\pi\)), Proposition 4.12 gives \(n^{8\tau/3}\le(2n-1)^6<64n^6\) for every integer \(n\ge 1\), so \(8\tau/3\le 6\), that is, \(\phi(\langle 2,2,2\rangle)\le 2^{9/4}\). Since this holds for every \(\phi\in\Delta_\mathbb{F}\), Theorem 4.2 gives \(\omega_\mathbb{F}\le 9/4\).

For a fixed integer \(n\ge 2\), the first inequality of Proposition 4.12 and the upper bound (2_n_-1)<sup>6</sup> give, in the same way,

\(\omega_\mathbb{F}\le\frac{3\mathrm{log}(2n-1)}{\mathrm{log}\big(\frac{3n-1}{2}\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\frac{3k+1}{3k}\big)}.\)

For example \(\omega_\mathbb{F}<2.74\) for _n_=2, the bound of the example in Section 1.2.3, and \(\omega_\mathbb{F}<2.65\) for _n_=3.

## 4.5 Quadratic constraints on asymptotic spectrum of matrix multiplication

We now extend the analysis in Lemma 4.11 and Proposition 4.12 to the rectangular case, which we will use to prove Theorem 1.2 in Section 4.6. The proof ideas are essentially the same, but we need to take into account the ratios of the "weights" given to the three legs resulting from the definition of \(\omega_\mathbb{F}(a,b,c)\).

The following lemma generalises Lemma 4.11, which is the case _u=v=b_ and _r=s_=1.

**Lemma 4.13.** _Let_ \(a\ge 1\) _be an integer, and let_ \(g,h:\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{>0}\) _be concave functions such that_ \(2g(m)+h(m)\le g(3m+a-1)\) _and_ \(2h(m)+g(m)\le h(3m+a-1)\) _for every integer_ \(m\ge 1\)_. Then for all integers_ \(u,v,r,s\ge 1\),

\(\big(\frac{g(u+r)}{g(u)}\big)^s\big(\frac{h(v+s)}{h(v)}\big)^r\ge\big(\frac{D}{D-\frac{4rs}{r+s}}\big)^{r+s},\)

_where D_:=_u+v+r+s+a_-1.

_Proof._ Let _m_:=max(_u+r,v+s_) and \(\lambda:=\frac{g(m)+h(m)}{2m+a-1}>0\). By concavity and the first hypothesis, for every integer \(1\le k<m\),<tbc>

\(g(k+1)-g(k)\ge\frac{g(3m+a-1)-g(m)}{2m+a-1}\ge\lambda.\)

<tbc>Likewise, \(h(k+1)-h(k)\ge\lambda\). Writing _A_:=_g(u+r_) and _B_:=_h(v+s_), summing these difference bounds gives \(A-g(u)\ge r\lambda\) and \(B-h(v)\ge s\lambda\). Similarly, \(g(m)-A\ge(m-u-r)\lambda\). Doing the same for _h_, and then using that \(g(m)+h(m)=\lambda(2m+a-1)\), we also find<tbc>

\(A+B\le g(m)+h(m)-\lambda(2m-u-r-v-s)=\lambda D.\)

<tbc>By the weighted arithmetic-mean geometric-mean inequality,

\(\big(\frac{g(u)}{A}\big)^{s/(r+s)}\big(\frac{h(v)}{B}\big)^{r/(r+s)}\le\frac{1}{r+s}\big(s\frac{g(u)}{A}+r\frac{h(v)}{B}\big).\) (4.3)

We have seen that \(1-g(u)/A\ge r\lambda/A\) and \(1-h(v)/B\ge s\lambda/B\), and that \(\lambda D\ge A+B\). Using this and also \(A^{-1}+B^{-1}\ge 4/(A+B)\), Equation (4.3) can be upper bounded by

\(\frac{s(1-r\lambda/A)+r(1-s\lambda/B)}{r+s}=1-\frac{rs\lambda}{r+s}\left(\frac{1}{A}+\frac{1}{B}\right)\le 1-\frac{4rs}{(r+s)D}.\)

Taking reciprocals and raising to the power _r+s_ proves the result.

**Proposition 4.14.** _For every_ \(\phi\in\Delta_\mathbb{F}\) _and all real numbers_ \(x_1,x_2,x_3\ge 0\),<tbc>

\(\phi(\langle 1,1,2\rangle)^{x_2x_3}\phi(\langle 2,1,1\rangle)^{x_1x_3}\phi(\langle 1,2,1\rangle)^{x_1x_2}\le 2^{(x_1+x_2+x_3)^2/4}.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ Let _p_<sub>1</sub>, _p_<sub>2</sub> and _p_<sub>3</sub> be the logarithms of \(\phi(\langle 1,1,2\rangle)\), \(\phi(\langle 2,1,1\rangle)\) and \(\phi(\langle 1,2,1\rangle)\), and let _S=x_<sub>1</sub>+_x_<sub>2</sub>+_x_<sub>3</sub> and _B=p_<sub>1</sub>_x_<sub>2</sub>_x_<sub>3</sub>+_p_<sub>2</sub>_x_<sub>1</sub>_x_<sub>3</sub>+_p_<sub>3</sub>_x_<sub>1</sub>_x_<sub>2</sub>. Taking logarithms, the claim is \(4B\le S^2\). Both sides of \(4B\le S^2\) are homogeneous of degree 2 in (_x_<sub>1</sub>_,x_<sub>2</sub>_,x_<sub>3</sub>) and continuous, so we may assume that _x_<sub>1</sub>, _x_<sub>2</sub> and _x_<sub>3</sub> are positive integers. For every integer \(n\ge 1\), let<tbc>

\(G_n:=\prod_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3}\phi_\pi\big(nx_{\pi(1)},nx_{\pi(2)}\big)^{x_{\pi(3)}}.\)

<tbc>Since \(1\le\phi_\pi(a,b)<a+b\) (Lemma 4.10(i) for \(\phi_\pi\)) and \(\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3}x_{\pi(3)}=2S\), we have \(G_1\ge 1\) and \(G_n\le(nS)^{2S}\). For \(\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_3\) and \(a\in\{n,n+1\}\), let<tbc>

\(R_\sigma(a):=\frac{\phi_\sigma\big(ax_{\sigma(1)},(n+1)x_{\sigma(2)}\big)}{\phi_\sigma\big(ax_{\sigma(1)},nx_{\sigma(2)}\big)}\)

<tbc>be the growth factor of \(\phi_\sigma\) in the second argument, at the first argument \(ax_{\sigma(1)}\). Let \(\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3\). Using \(\phi_\pi(a,b)=\phi_{\pi\circ(12)}(b,a)\) we find<tbc>

\(\frac{\phi_\pi\big((n+1)x_{\pi(1)},(n+1)x_{\pi(2)}\big)}{\phi_\pi\big(nx_{\pi(1)},nx_{\pi(2)}\big)}=R_\pi(n+1)R_{\pi\circ(12)}(n).\)

<tbc>We raise this to the power \(x_{\pi(3)}\), which equals \(x_{(\pi\circ(12))(3)}\), and multiply over \(\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_3\). Since \(\pi\mapsto\pi\circ(12)\) is a bijection of S<sub>3</sub>, this gives<tbc>

\(\frac{G_{n+1}}{G_n}=\prod_{a\in\{n,n+1\}}\prod_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_3}R_\sigma(a)^{x_{\sigma(3)}}.\)

<tbc>The six permutations form three pairs \(\{\sigma,\sigma\circ(23)\}\), one for each \(i\in\{1,2,3\}\), with \(\sigma(1)=i\). Let \(j=\sigma(2)\) and \(k=\sigma(3)\). Let \(a\in\{n,n+1\}\). If _p<sub>i</sub>\>_0, then by Lemma 4.10, applied to \(\phi_\sigma\) and \(\phi_{\sigma\circ(23)}\), the functions \(m\mapsto\phi_\sigma(ax_i,m)^{1/p_i}\) and \(m\mapsto\phi_{\sigma\circ(23)}(ax_i,m)^{1/p_i}\) satisfy the hypotheses of Lemma 4.13 with _ax<sub>i</sub>_ in place of _a_. Here we use that both spectral points take the value 2_<sup>p<sub>i</sub></sup>_ at \(\langle 1,1,2\rangle\), since \(\sigma\) and \(\sigma\circ(23)\) move its one-dimensional first leg to leg _i_, and that \(\phi_\sigma((23)\cdot T)=\phi_{\sigma\circ(23)}(T)\) and \(\phi_{\sigma\circ(23)}((23)\cdot T)=\phi_\sigma(T)\) for every tensor _T_, since \(\pi\cdot(\rho\cdot T)=(\pi\circ\rho)\cdot T\) for all \(\pi,\rho\in\mathfrak{S}_3\). That lemma with _u=nx<sub>j</sub>_, _v=nx<sub>k</sub>_, _r=x<sub>j</sub>_ and _s=x<sub>k</sub>_, raised to the power _p<sub>i</sub>_, gives<tbc>

\(R_\sigma(a)^{x_k}R_{\sigma\circ(23)}(a)^{x_j}\ge\big(\frac{D}{D-c}\big)^{p_i(x_j+x_k)},\)

<tbc>where _D_=(_n_+1)(_x<sub>j</sub>+x<sub>k</sub>_)+_ax<sub>i</sub>_-1 and _c_=4_x<sub>j</sub>x<sub>k</sub>/(x<sub>j</sub>+x<sub>k</sub>)\>_0. Since \(D\le(n+1)S\) and \(t:=c/S\le(x_j+x_k)/S\le 1\), we find, using Bernoulli’s inequality (which says that \((1+y)^t\le 1+ty\) for every real number \(0\le t\le 1\) and \(y\ge-1\)) in the last step, that<tbc>

\(\frac{D}{D-c}\ge 1+\frac{c}{D}\ge 1+\frac{t}{n+1}\ge\big(\frac{n+2}{n+1}\big)^t.\)

Since _tp<sub>i</sub>(x<sub>j</sub>+x<sub>k</sub>_)=4_p<sub>i</sub>x<sub>j</sub>x<sub>k</sub>/S_, we obtain<tbc>

\(R_\sigma(a)^{x_k}R_{\sigma\circ(23)}(a)^{x_j}\ge\big(\frac{n+2}{n+1}\big)^{4p_ix_jx_k/S}.\)

<tbc>If _p<sub>i</sub>_=0, this lower bound holds as well, since the left-hand side is at least 1: \(\phi_\sigma\) and \(\phi_{\sigma\circ(23)}\) are nondecreasing in the second argument (Lemma 4.10(i)). Multiplying over the three pairs and the two values of _a_ gives

\(\frac{G_{n+1}}{G_n}\ge\big(\frac{n+2}{n+1}\big)^{8B/S},\text{so}G_n\ge\big(\frac{n+1}{2}\big)^{8B/S},\)

where we multiply these inequalities and use \(G_1\ge 1\). With the upper bound on _G<sub>n</sub>_, this gives \(((n+1)/2)^{8B/S}\le(nS)^{2S}\) for every integer \(n\ge 1\). Hence \(8B/S\le 2S\), that is, \(4B\le S^2\).

Proposition 4.14 gives an "outer approximation" of the asymptotic spectrum of rectangular matrix multiplication, which we plot in Figure 4. To explain this, let<tbc>

\(\Delta_\mathbb{F}^\mathfrak{m}:=\big\{\big(\phi(\langle 1,1,2\rangle),\phi(\langle 2,1,1\rangle),\phi(\langle 1,2,1\rangle)\big):\phi\in\Delta_\mathbb{F}\big\}\subseteq[1,2]^3\)

## 5 Operational barrier

In this section we will prove that no combination of the ingredients (D0)-(D4) by the rules (C1)-(C4) improves the bounds of Theorem 1.2.

To do this, we will define a semiring F of formal combinations of the polynomial multiplication tensors and their permutations, under \(\oplus\), \(\otimes\) and the partial direct sums \(\oplus_i\) (which are not semiring operations, and are only allowed under the natural leg dimension constraint). By "formal combinations" here we mean that we do not a priori identify restriction equivalent or isomorphic tensors. Instead, we define a special preorder \(\unknown\) on F which only encodes the degeneration ingredients (D0)-(D4) and combination rules (C1)-(C4) that we use in the proofs of Theorem 1.2. Thus any degeneration construction from those ingredients and rules can be written in the preorder \(\unknown\).

To prove no degenerations \(\langle n,n,n\rangle\unknown\langle r\rangle\) give log_r/_log_n\<_9/4, the natural approach would be to find a degeneration monotone function \(\phi\) that obstructs \(\langle n,n,n\rangle\unknown\langle r\rangle\) in the sense that \(\phi(\langle n,n,n\rangle)>\phi(\langle r\rangle)\) whenever log_r/_log_n\<_9/4.

In fact, more abstractly, one may take such \(\phi\) in the asymptotic spectrum \(\Delta_\mathbb{F}\) and use \(\mathrm{max}_{\phi\in\Delta_\mathbb{F}}\phi(\langle 2,2,2\rangle)=2^{\omega_\mathbb{F}}\); that is, if \(\omega_\mathbb{F}=9/4\), then there is a \(\phi\in\Delta_\mathbb{F}\) such that \(\phi(\langle 2,2,2\rangle)=2^{9/4}\), and then \(\phi(\langle n,n,n\rangle)=n^{9/4}\) by basic powering arguments.

We do not know how to obtain such a degeneration monotone \(\phi\); instead, we will restrict ourselves to only work with the semiring of formal expression F and the restricted operational preorder \(\unknown\) on F. We will then construct functions \(F_\theta^\star\) on F that are \(\unknown\)-monotone (they are in fact in the asymptotic spectrum of \((\mathcal{F},\unknown)\)). These functions \(F_\theta^\star\) are constructed in a way that they obstruct all \(\langle n,n,n\rangle\unknown\langle r\rangle\) that can lead to \(\omega_\mathbb{F}<9/4\) (and similarly for the rectangular bounds). This "operational barrier" result is Theorem 5.4.

The challenge lies in constructing the functions \(F_\theta^\star\) as above, which we do in Section 5.4, and prove their monotonicity in Section 5.6 and Section 5.7.

This construction also gives a test for usefulness of different sets of degeneration ingredients to obtain better bounds on \(\omega_\mathbb{F}\): adding them to \(\unknown\) keeps the barrier whenever the functions \(F_\theta^\star\) remain monotone. This we state in Proposition 5.7.

## 5.1 Symmetric notation P_<sub>x,y,z</sub>_ for permuted polynomial multiplication

For convenience in this section, we will use a more symmetric notation for polynomial multiplication tensors and their permutations, \(\pi\cdot\mathsf{P}_{a,b}\). To see how this is natural, recall

\(\mathsf{P}_{a,b}=\sum_{i=1}^a\sum_{j=1}^be_i\otimes e_j\otimes e_{i+j-1}.\)

The terms are of the form \(e_i\otimes e_j\otimes e_k\) with \(i\in[a]\), \(j\in[b]\), \(k\in[a+b-1]\) such that _i+j-k_=1. Replacing _k_ by _a+b-k_ turns the condition _i+j-k_=1 into _i+j+k=a+b_+1=_M_+2, where _M=a+b_-1 is the largest of the three leg dimensions of P_<sub>a,b</sub>_. This definition is more symmetric and is what we use in the following:

**Definition 5.1.** A triple (_x,y,z_) of real numbers \(x,y,z\ge 1\) is _admissible_ if<tbc>

\(x+y+z=2\mathrm{max}(x,y,z)+1,\)

<tbc>that is, if its largest entry is the sum of the other two minus 1. For an admissible triple of integers, with _M_=max(_x,y,z_), let

Similarly, each \(F_\theta^\star\) is also monotone on the polynomial multiplication degenerations of Remark 3.10 and Remark 3.12, so the barrier applies. As another example, which is also clear form the asymptotic spectrum point of view, the barrier remains true if \(\unknown\) is replaced by its asymptotic closure. There an expression \(T\in\mathcal{F}\) is at most \(S\in\mathcal{F}\) if \(T^{\otimes n}\unknown S^{\otimes n}\otimes\langle 2^{o(n)}\rangle\) for every integer \(n\ge 1\). Indeed, then \(F_\theta^\star(T)^n\le F_\theta^\star(S)^n2^{o(n)}\) for every integer \(n\ge 1\), since \(F_\theta^\star\) is multiplicative and \(F_\theta^\star(\langle 2^{o(n)}\rangle)=2^{o(n)}\), so \(F_\theta^\star(T)\le F_\theta^\star(S)\).

## 5.8 Operational asymptotic spectrum \(\Delta_\unknown\)

Let \(\Delta_\unknown\) be the set of functions \(F:\mathcal{F}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{>0}\) with \(F(\langle 1\rangle)=1\), \(F(S\oplus T)=F(S)+F(T)\) and \(F(S\otimes T)=F(S)F(T)\) for all \(S,T\in\mathcal{F}\), and with \(F(T)\le F(S)\) whenever \(T\unknown S\). This is the asymptotic spectrum of the semiring of ≈-classes of F, ordered by \(\unknown\), where _T≈S_ if \(T\unknown S\) and \(S\unknown T\).

The following theorem phrases the barrier results in the language of this asymptotic spectrum \(\Delta_\unknown\).

**Theorem 5.11** (Maximum over \(\Delta_\unknown\))**.** _For all real numbers_ \(a\ge b\ge c\ge 0\),

\(\mathrm{max}_{F\in\Delta_\unknown} F(\langle 2,1,1\rangle)^aF(\langle 1,2,1\rangle)^bF(\langle 1,1,2\rangle)^c=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
2^{a+b} & \text{\textit{if}}c(a+b)\le ab, \\
2^{(ab+bc+ca)^2/(4abc)} & \text{\textit{if}}c(a+b)>ab.
\end{array}\right.\)

_In particular,_ \(\mathrm{max}_{F\in\Delta_\unknown} F(\langle 2,2,2\rangle)=2^{9/4}\).

_Proof._ We sketch the proof. The central idea is that in the proof of Theorem 1.2, the properties of spectral points that are used are exactly the ones in the definition of \(\Delta_\unknown\). This establishes the upper bound (we provide a bit more detail below).

These upper bounds are subsequently attained by \(F_\theta^\star\) with the parameters of Lemma 5.6 (in the second case) and by the flattening rank R<sub>(1)</sub> (in the first case). We obtain equality because \(F_\theta^\star\in\Delta_\unknown\) (by its definition and Proposition 5.9) and \(\mathrm{R}_{(1)}\in\Delta_\unknown\) (because every relation in \(\unknown\) is a degeneration).

We now provide some more details on the upper bound. Let \(F\in\Delta_\unknown\). The proof of Proposition 4.14 uses several properties of spectral points concerning their evaluations at the tensors P_<sub>x,y,z</sub>_, and _F_ also satisfy these properties. First, _F_(P<sub>1_,m,m_</sub>)=_m<sup>p</sup>_ with _p_=log\(F(\mathsf{P}_{1,2,2})\in[0,1]\) for all \(m\ge 1\), which is the case because \(m\mapsto F(\mathsf{P}_{1,m,m})\) is multiplicative by (I3), nondecreasing by (R2) and at most _m_ by (D1). Second, \(F(\mathsf{P}_{x,y,z})\ge F(\langle 1\rangle)=1\), which follows from (R2).

Finally, the properties in Lemma 4.10, which follow from (D1)-(D4), (R) and (I) by the proofs of Lemma 4.5, Lemma 4.6 and Lemma 4.10. Zooming in on the proof of Lemma 4.5, we see that it uses that the summands are isomorphic only to compute the value of their direct sum; for _F_, additivity gives \(F(U_1\oplus\cdots\oplus U_r)=rF(U_1)\) whenever \(F(U_1)=\cdots=F(U_r)\), so that proof applies to summands with equal values of _F_. In the proof of Lemma 4.6, the summands of one type have equal values of _F_, since _F_ is multiplicative.

These are all the properties that are used in proof of Proposition 4.14 and Lemma 4.15, and hence also in the proof of Theorem 1.2. We conclude the upper bound applies.

Let \(\Delta_\unknown^\mathsf{m}:=\big\{\big(F(\langle 1,1,2\rangle),F(\langle 2,1,1\rangle),F(\langle 1,2,1\rangle)\big):F\in\Delta_\unknown\big\}\). Then \(\mathrm{log}\Delta_\mathbb{F}^\mathsf{m}\subseteq\mathrm{log}\Delta_\unknown^\mathsf{m}\subseteq Q\), for the set _Q_ of (4.4), since every relation in \(\unknown\) is a degeneration and since the proof of Theorem 5.11 shows the inequality of Proposition 4.14 for every \(F\in\Delta_\unknown\).
